scenes.script_line: Imagine you have finished opening a package at work. Inside is the part you need. Outside is a little piece of plastic. You take the part. You start working. And the plastic falls to the ground. It is small. It seems unimportant. Perhaps you think, "Someone will pick it up later." But today, I want to ask you one simple question. When we throw something away, where does it actually go?

shots.text: worker opening a delivery package on site, a small plastic strip falling free
close-up of a small plastic strip landing on the ground
wide shot of a morning worksite with crates and tools being unpacked
worker continuing to work, not noticing the fallen plastic behind them

scenes.script_line: Think about that word: away. Where is away? When the wind moves a wrapper, it has not disappeared. When rain carries a piece of plastic into a ditch, it has not disappeared. When rubbish is hidden beneath leaves, it has not disappeared. It has only moved from one place to another. This is the first idea to remember.

shots.text: close-up of a light plastic wrapper being lifted and carried by wind
wide shot of dry open ground with a wrapper blowing across it
wrapper settling into a drainage ditch beside a path
close-up of rubbish partly hidden beneath fallen leaves

scenes.script_line: There is no place called away. Let's say it again. There is no place called away. Imagine rain falling on a building site. Some of it enters the soil. Some flows downhill. Along the way, moving water can carry small pieces of rubbish. A wrapper that started beside a wall may reach a ditch. From there, it may travel toward a stream or another waterway. Not every piece follows that journey.

shots.text: wide shot of rain falling across a sloped building site
water running downhill along a shallow channel carrying small debris
close-up of a small piece of rubbish moving with flowing water
wide shot of a stream at the edge of the estate after rain

scenes.script_line: But once rubbish escapes, we no longer control where it goes. And what looked like a tiny problem in one corner can become a problem somewhere else. Now think about a cigarette butt. Some people imagine that the filter is made of cotton. Most conventional cigarette filters are actually made from a type of plastic.

shots.text: medium shot of a worker looking down at an empty corner where rubbish has escaped
close-up of a cigarette filter on a clean surface showing its fibres
worker safely extinguishing a cigarette in a proper receptacle
wide shot of dry ground with a small marked smoking area sign post

scenes.script_line: They can remain in the environment and break into smaller pieces. And a cigarette that has not been fully extinguished can also start a fire. On dry land, that is a serious risk. One small object. More than one possible consequence. That is why we never leave cigarette butts on the ground at Edenrise. We follow the site's smoking restrictions, and where smoking is permitted, we use the correct safe receptacle.

shots.text: two workstations side by side, one scattered with wrappers, one tidy and sorted
shots.pexels: two workstations one tidy one messy

shots.text: worker placing a wrapper straight into a correct waste container
close-up of hands sorting different waste into labelled containers
wide shot of a row of clearly marked waste bins on site

scenes.script_line: Now imagine two workers. Both have opened ten boxes and fitted ten pieces of equipment. The first worker leaves the wrappers where they fall. The second puts them straight into the correct waste container. Which worker has finished the job properly? Which work area is safer when the wind begins to blow? Which worker makes the next person's job easier? The difference is not talent. It is a small choice, repeated throughout the day.

shots.text: worker asking a supervisor a question beside a waste sorting area
close-up of a hand pointing to a clearly marked waste label
worker safely picking up a plastic tie from a path and placing it in a container
wide shot of a well-organised site with separated waste streams visible

scenes.script_line: And there is another important point. Not every kind of waste belongs in the same bin. Clean packaging, reusable offcuts, construction debris and hazardous materials may need different handling. If you are unsure, ask your supervisor. Guessing is not the same as disposing of something correctly. At Edenrise, the company must provide clearly marked places for waste. And each of us must use them.

shots.text: close-up of hands carefully avoiding a sharp object on the ground
worker reporting something to a supervisor using a radio or gesture
medium shot of a worker double-checking before leaving a work area
wide shot of a clean finished corner of the site at the end of the day

scenes.script_line: You do not need to solve the world's waste problem today. You can begin with what is in front of you. Notice it. Collect it safely. Put it in the right place. Notice. Collect. Separate. Let's repeat. Notice. Collect. Separate. If something is sharp, contaminated or dangerous, do not pick it up without the right training and equipment. Report it.

shots.text: worker notices a sharp or hazardous item and steps back instead of touching it
close-up of a hand gesturing for a colleague to keep distance from a hazard
trained worker in protective gloves safely collecting a sharp object
wide shot of a supervisor walking toward a reported trouble spot on site

scenes.script_line: Responsibility also means knowing when to ask for help. Tomorrow, when you finish using a material, ask yourself: "Where will the packaging go?" And before you leave your work area, ask: "Is anything left here that could travel somewhere else?" Because throwing something away does not make it disappear. It always goes somewhere. In the next lesson, we will look beneath our feet and discover why protecting the soil matters just as much as keeping its surface clean.

shots.text: worker pausing at the end of a task, looking around the work area
close-up of empty packaging being placed into a labelled bin by hand
wide shot of a tidy work area left clean at the end of the day
worker glancing back one more time before leaving the site
